d: Make less visible or unclear
ety: From be- + cloud.
s: Day light began to forsake the red-room; it was past four o’clock, and the beclouded afternoon was tending to drear twilight.

d: A member of an armed gang of robbers
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani ڈکیت / डकैत (ḍakait), from ڈاکا (ḍākā) / डाका (ḍākā, “gang-robbery”).
s: On the way back Boyles led him down a lampless lane, and sure enough, a pair of dacoits pounced on them.

d: Easily irritated or annoyed
ety: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English pievish, peuysche, pevish, pevysh (“capricious, wilful; perverse, wayward”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from one of the following: * From an unattested Old French word, from Latin perversus (“corrupted, perverted, subverted; overthrown”), the perfect passive participle of pervertō (“to corrupt, subvert; to overthrow”), from per- (prefix
s: I would rather figure things out on my own than ask that peevish librarian for help.

d: Argumentation that is specious or excessively subtle and intended to be misleading
ety: From casuist + -ry.
s: “And if you lose?” Diana enunciated, through a thin grin. She meant to extract casuistry’s penalty in advance.

d: Gnaw into; make resentful or angry
ety: From Middle English ranklen, ranclen, from Old French rancler, räoncler, draoncler (“to ulcerate, to form a boil”), from Old French draoncle (“a boil”), from Latin dracunculus (“little serpent”), diminutive of Latin dracō (“serpent, dragon”).
s: My colleague's gratuitous criticism still rankles with me.

d: Wrangle (over a price, terms of an agreement, etc.)
ety: From Middle English chaffare (“a bargain, a trade”, noun), equivalent to cheap + fare.
s: To chaffer for preferment with his gold.

d: Use of a word to govern two or more words though appropriate to only one
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ζεῦγμα (zeûgma, “yoking; a bond, a band”), from ζεύγνυμι (zeúgnumi, “to yoke; to join”), from ζεῦγος (zeûgos, “a yoke”).
s: `Mr. Pickwick took his hat and his leave' is an example of zeugma.

d: Physically and mentally fatigued
ety: From a- + weary.
s: "Nay, save that she seems aweary".

d: Overabundance of words
ety: From French verbiage. Compare verb meaning "word" in verbal and verbose.
s: We're done drafting our paper except for the final check to see whether any verbiage can be reduced.

d: Polished courtesy; elegance of manner
ety: From Middle English urbanitie, from Middle French urbanité, from Latin urbānitās, from urbānus (“belonging to a city”), with a sense of "having the manners of townspeople" in Classical Latin, from urbs (“city”); equivalent to urbane + -ity (sense 1) and urban + -ity (sense 2).
s: Wealdon's two little visits explained perfectly the active urbanities of Captain Stanley Lake.

d: A morbid fear of the number 13
ety: From triskaideka- (“thirteen”) + -phobia.
s: There’s even a name to describe the irrational dread of the date: paraskevidekatriaphobia — a specialized form of triskaidekaphobia, a fear of the number 13.

d: Effusively or insincerely emotional
ety: From bathos + -etic, based on the form of pathos and pathetic.
s: The fall is indeed the archetypal bathetic motion, a sudden, surprising downward rush degrading the pretensions of posture and man's bipedal pride.

d: Bitter or scornful
ety: From Middle English saturnine, satournine, satournyne, saturnin, saturnyn, saturnyne (“pertaining to or under the influence of the planet Saturn; line on the palm of the hand associated with Saturn”), from Old French saturnine, saturnin (modern French saturnin (“of, pertaining to, resembling or containing lead, plumbic”)), or directly from its etymon Medieval Latin Sāturnīnus, from Sāturnus (“the
s: The monstrous thought came into my mind as I perused the fixed eyes and the saturnine face, that this was a spirit, not a man.

d: Difficult to penetrate; incomprehensible to one of ordinary understanding or knowledge
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin abstrūsus (“concealed, hidden; having been concealed”), an adjective use of the perfect passive participle of abstrūdō (“to conceal, hide; to push or thrust away”), from abs- (from ab- (prefix meaning ‘away; from; away from’)) + trūdō (“to push, shove; to thrust”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to push; to thrust”)). Cognates * Catalan abstrús * German
s: In a thousand ways he smoothed for me the path of knowledge, and made the most abstruse inquiries clear and facile to my apprehension.

d: The left side of a ship or aircraft to someone who is aboard and facing the bow or nose
ety: From Middle English ladde-bord, latebord, most likely referring to the side of the ship on which cargo was loaded. Changed to larboard in the 1500s by association with starboard. (Texts from the 1500s have spellings like lerbord, leereboord, larboord, corresponding to how they spell sterbord, steereboord, starboord.)
s: "It means to turn to larboard."

d: Excessively agitated; distraught with fear or other violent emotion
ety: From Middle English frenetik (also frentik, frentyk, frantike > modern English frantic), from Old French frenetike, from Latin phreneticus, from Ancient Greek φρενητικός (phrenētikós, “delirious”), from φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “delirium”), from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”). Doublet of frantic and phrenitic. Etymologically, initial stress would be expected (compare the syncopic form phrentic); the modern pron
s: After a week of working at a frenetic pace, she was ready for Saturday.

d: Express one’s sympathetic grief, on the occasion of someone’s death
s: She condoled with her father over the death of his mother.

d: Shaped like a ring
ety: From Latin ānulāris (“ring-shaped”); (possibly through French annulaire), from ānulus (“ring”).
s: If anybody snickers, put 'em in their place by reminding them that the annular wing is a very old aeronautical principle.

d: Ostentatiously lofty in style
ety: From Latin turgidus (“swollen, inflated”), from turgeō (“to swell”).
s: The Jiet River lay before them, as thick and turgid as a gorged snake, its crosshatched surface reflecting the same ghastly hue that pervaded the Burning Plains.

d: A vote by the electorate determining public opinion on a question of national importance
ety: Sense 1 (“referendum”) is borrowed from French plébiscite, from Latin plēbiscītum, plēbis scītum, plēbī scītum (“law of the common people or plebs”), from plēbis (the genitive singular of plēbs (“common people, plebeians”)) + scītum (“decree, ordinance, statute”). Sense 3 (“law enacted by the common people”) is a learned borrowing from Latin plēbiscītum: see above. It is attested earlier than Engl
s: A political result, we may also say aim, of the frumentarian plebiscite of Gaius was to disattach the city populace from its conservative moorings and to enlist it in the service of reform.

d: Relevant and appropriate
ety: A variant form of german (“having the same parents; related”), adapted in this sense in allusions to its use in Shakespeare's Hamlet (see quotations at germaine).
s: 1924, W. D. Ross., translator, Aristotle, Metaphysics. Nashotah, Wisconsin, USA: The Classical Library, 2001, Book 1, Part 5. Yet this much is germane to the present inquiry:

d: A guide who conducts and informs sightseers
ety: 1726, from Italian cicerone (surface analysis cicero + -one (augmentative)), from Latin Cicerōnem, form of Cicerō, agnomen of Marcus Tullius Cicero), the Roman orator, from cicer (“chickpea”) from Proto-Indo-European *ḱiker- (“pea”). Possibly humorous reference to loquaciousness of guides.
s: Ultimately their gazes all rested on his cicerone as most powerful member of the group.

d: Having or exerting a malignant influence
ety: From Latin maleficus.
s: I would have liked to know whether he thought this was due to the climate, the diet, or simply malefic djinns.

d: Armor plate that protects legs below the knee
ety: From Middle English greve, from Old English grǣfe, grǣfa (“bush, bramble, grove, thicket, copse, brush-wood (for burning), fuel”). Cognate with Scots greve, greave (“grove”). Compare also Proto-Germanic *grainiz (“twig”), of unknown origin, whence Old Norse grein (“branch, bough”). Closely related to Old English grāf, grāfa (“grove”). See grove.
s: Then he cast off his breast-plate, thigh pieces, and greaves, while Alleyne followed his example.

d: A girl who behaves in a boyish manner
ety: Probably from Middle Dutch heyden (“heathen, gypsy”), heidin (Modern Dutch heiden).
s: Tabitha is lighting the candles in the sconces. A great, strong, heavy girl, a hoyden, not pretty, her face distinguished only by youth, by health.

d: Someone skilled in the transcription of speech (especially dictation)
ety: From Latin āmanuēnsis (“secretary”), from ab- (“from, off (of)”) + manus (“hand”) + -ensis (“of or from (a place)”), early 17th c.
s: I, his mere amanuensis, am left to do what little I can to keep the institution functioning.

d: Blatant or sensational promotion
ety: Earlier houp-la, hoop la, first attested in c. 1877, probably from French houp-là, oup-là (“upsadaisy, upsy-daisy”), a cry to various animals close to humans like horses and dogs, of likely onomatopoeic origin (but see là). Compare interjections like whoop, ahoy, hoo.
s: Campers enjoyed all of the traditional camp hoopla: color wars, shared team games with other camps and young eager college students spending their summer as counselors.

d: A reward or payment
ety: From Middle English guerdon, guerdoun, gardone, from Old French guerdon, guerredon, guarredon, werdon, from Medieval Latin widerdōnum, alteration of widerlōnum, from West Germanic (whence Old High German widarlōn, Old English wiþerlēan), literally ‘back-payment’, with the second element assimilated to Latin dōnum (“gift”).
s: Verse, like the laurel its immortal meed, Should be the guerdon of a noble deed

d: A dirty shabbily clothed urchin
ety: From the Middle English Ragamuffyn. Of uncertain origin, according to Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable: A muffin is a poor thing of a creature, a ‘regular muff’; so that a ragamuffin is a sorry creature in rags.
s: A boy of the cheery gypsy ragamuffin variety.

d: To agree or express agreement
ety: Borrowed from Middle French acquiescer, from Latin acquiescō; ad + quiescō (“to rest”), from quies (“rest”).
s: They were compelled to acquiesce in a government which they did not regard as just.

d: Someone or something that is abnormally large and powerful
ety: From Middle English behemoth, bemoth, from Late Latin behemoth, from Hebrew בְּהֵמוֹת (behemót). Most likely, the Hebrew word is an intensive plural of בְּהֵמָה (behemá, “beast”), from Proto-Semitic (compare Ge'ez ብህመ (bəhmä, “to be dumb, to be speechless”), Arabic ب ه م (b h m)). Some have instead suggested a borrowing from a hypothetical Egyptian pA-i-H-E1-mw (*pꜣ-jḥ-mw, “hippopotamus”, literall
s: The wide access corridors passed slowly, the conduits and pipes like the circulatory system of some vast planetary behemoth.

d: Immoderately desirous of acquiring e.g. wealth
ety: From Middle English avaricious, from Old French avaricieux, from avarice, from Latin avaritia (“greed”), from avarus (“greedy”), of avere (“crave, long for”).
s: In a word, he was called a hard, avaricious, rapacious man, whose chief business was to enrich himself...

d: A bell attached to a sleigh, or to the harness of a horse that is pulling a sleigh
ety: Borrowed from Spanish cascabel (“bell, rattle”).
s: Prepare the cascabels using one of the methods in the Preparing Cascabels box, at left.

d: One who lives in solitude
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Trōglodytae (“cave-dwelling people”), from Ancient Greek τρωγλοδύτης (trōglodútēs, “one who dwells in holes”), from τρώγλη (trṓglē, “hole”) + δύω (dúō, “to get into”).
s: The cave was populated by albino scorpions, blind salamanders, and other troglodytes.

d: A broad cartridge belt worn over the shoulder by soldiers
ety: From earlier form bandollier, from Middle French bandoulliere, from Catalan bandolera, feminine derivative of bandoler (“member of a band of men”), from Catalan bàndol (“band, faction, party”), from Old Spanish bando.
s: We had each bandoliers of cartridges.

d: Having no known beginning and presumably no end
ety: From Old French sempiternel, from Medieval Latin sempiternālis, from Latin sempiternus, a contraction of semperæternus, from semper (“always”) + æternus (“eternal”).
s: Why not sempiternal / Thou and I? Our vernal / Brightness keeping, / Time outleaping: / Passed the hodiernal!

d: Unpredictably excitable (especially of horses)
ety: Probably from skite (“to move lightly and hurriedly; to move suddenly, particularly in an oblique direction (Scotland, Northern England)”) + -ish; compare skitter.
s: The dog likes people he knows, but he is skittish around strangers.

d: A state or atmosphere of harmony or mutual civility and respect
ety: From Late Middle English comite (“association”), from Latin cōmitās.
s: Comity and conciliation are a slog. They’re for suckers. Contempt is victors’ ready, heady prerogative.

d: A small overnight bag for short trips
ety: Borrowed from French valise.
s: Nothing to declare / Not in the valise of my mind

d: Argue over petty things
ety: Back-formation from pettifogger.
s: Don't pettifog or we will soon grow weary.
